claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles depends on synchronized precursor conversion.
Synchronized precursor conversion produces a transient multimetallic intermediate.
The transient multimetallic intermediate acts as a homogenizing scaffold.
Nearly simultaneous conversion of all metal precursors leads to nucleation of a uniform alloy phase.
Mismatched precursor conversion leads to phase separation, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled morphology.
The proposed intervention promotes synchronous precursor conversion.
A rapid conversion pathway minimizes temporal differences among precursor-reduction events.
The proposed synthesis conditions are scalable and cost-effective.
The transient intermediate forms during the early reaction stages and facilitates uniform nucleation and atomic mixing.
The transient intermediate allows metal atoms to interdiffuse before crystallization.
Early formation of one metallic phase under asynchronous reduction causes phase segregation and morphology-control problems.
Relative to baseline synthesis, the intervention will produce nanoparticles with a more uniform elemental distribution.
Relative to baseline synthesis, the intervention will produce more controlled nanoparticle morphology.
Relative to baseline synthesis, the intervention will preserve high surface-atom exposure.
The baseline has unsynchronized precursor-conversion kinetics that result in phase separation or uncontrolled morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal systems whose constituent metals have sufficiently similar reduction potentials to permit simultaneous conversion.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to systems with vastly disparate reduction kinetics.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to non-noble-metal systems in which other factors dominate particle formation.
